What Is Node.js?

JavaScript running outside the browser, and why that matters for building a server.

Until now, every line of JavaScript you've written has run inside a browser — triggered by a page load, a click, a form submit. Node.js is the same JavaScript language, but running as a standalone program on a machine, with no browser involved at all. There's no window, no document, no DOM — just JavaScript with access to the machine it's running on: the filesystem, the network, environment variables.

That's what makes it possible to write a web server in JavaScript rather than only a web page. Where Laravel gave you PHP running inside Apache/nginx via PHP-FPM, Node is the server process — there's no separate web server handing requests to it up front. A Node process you start yourself listens on a port and handles requests directly.

You run a JavaScript file with Node from the command line, the same way you'd run a PHP script with php:

node some-file.js

Node executes the file top to bottom and exits — unless the code keeps something running, like a server listening for connections. That's exactly what src/server.js will do shortly: start a process that doesn't exit, because it's sitting there waiting for HTTP requests.

One more mental shift worth flagging now, because it matters a lot for how this API's code will behave: a PHP-FPM worker starts fresh for every request — no variable survives from one request to the next unless it's in the database or a session. A Node process, by contrast, keeps running and keeps its memory across every request it handles, until you stop it. We'll come back to exactly why that matters once there's code that depends on it.
